name: Gliese 12 b
significanceText: The nearest known transiting, temperate, Earth-sized world to us — just 40 light-years away — making it one of the best real-world targets for testing whether small rocky planets around red dwarfs can hold onto an atmosphere.

name: K2-133 e
significanceText: The outermost of five tightly packed super-Earths circling a cool dwarf star, sitting closest to the temperate part of its system and offering a look at how planet size and spacing evolve across a single compact system.

name: K2-18 b
significanceText: A mini-Neptune in its star's habitable zone that made headlines when JWST detected methane and carbon dioxide in its atmosphere — and, more controversially, a possible biosignature gas — reshaping the debate over "Hycean" ocean worlds.

name: K2-3 d
significanceText: The outermost of three super-Earths around a nearby red dwarf, orbiting right where temperatures could allow liquid water, and a frequently cited benchmark in surveys of compact multi-planet systems around M dwarfs.

name: Kepler-155 c
significanceText: A Neptune-sized world orbiting a K-type star, useful as a comparison case for how planet composition changes at the boundary between rocky super-Earths and gas-rich mini-Neptunes.

name: Kepler-186 e
significanceText: One of four close-in siblings to the famous habitable-zone world Kepler-186f, this planet sits just inside the system's warm edge and helps map out exactly where the habitable zone begins around a red dwarf.

name: Kepler-22 b
significanceText: The first exoplanet ever confirmed orbiting in the habitable zone of a genuinely Sun-like star, marking a milestone moment for the Kepler mission even though its larger size suggests an ocean world rather than a rocky twin.

name: Kepler-249 d
significanceText: The outermost of three small planets tightly orbiting a cool dwarf star, offering another data point on how common multi-planet systems are around low-mass stars.

name: Kepler-296 e
significanceText: One of two habitable-zone super-Earths in the Kepler-296 system, discovered in the same 2014 haul that nearly doubled Kepler's confirmed planet count and highlighted how often small worlds cluster in temperate orbits.

name: Kepler-296 f
significanceText: The outer of two habitable-zone worlds around Kepler-296, flagged among the very first small planets confirmed inside a star's habitable zone using a statistical "verification by multiplicity" technique rather than individual follow-up.

name: Kepler-445 d
significanceText: A compact super-Earth in a tightly packed system around a red dwarf, part of a wave of small Kepler worlds that helped establish just how crowded planetary systems around M dwarfs can be.

name: Kepler-69 c
significanceText: Once announced as a potential habitable-zone world, later reanalysis pushed it just outside the zone into Venus-like territory — a reminder of how habitable-zone boundaries get revised as models improve, earning it the informal tag "super-Venus."

name: LHS 1903 e
significanceText: The outer rocky world in a strange "inside-out" four-planet system where two gas-rich planets sit sandwiched between two rocky ones — a configuration that upends the usual rocky-close, gassy-far pattern and challenges standard planet-formation models.

name: TOI-1452 b
significanceText: A super-Earth dense enough, relative to its size, that astronomers suspect it could be a genuine "ocean world" with a deep global sea beneath its atmosphere — one of the most compelling water-world candidates found to date.

name: TOI-2094 b
significanceText: A super-Earth sitting right at the edge of its star's habitable zone, straddling the line between a rocky world and a gas-rich mini-Neptune depending on which mass estimate turns out to be correct.

name: TOI-2267 c
significanceText: Part of the first confirmed binary system found hosting transiting planets around both of its stars — an ultra-compact, ultra-cold pairing that defies predictions that such tight binaries should make planet formation impossible.

name: TOI-6002 b
significanceText: A super-Earth sitting almost exactly on the "radius valley" — the size gap separating rocky super-Earths from puffier mini-Neptunes — making it a useful test case for theories of atmospheric loss around small stars.

name: TOI-6716 b
significanceText: A near-Earth-size, near-Earth-mass world orbiting a mid-M dwarf, discovered as part of a dedicated survey to precisely measure temperate planets around small, fully convective stars.

name: TOI-700 d
significanceText: The first Earth-size habitable-zone planet ever found by TESS, confirmed with backup observations from the Spitzer Space Telescope and celebrated as a landmark win for NASA's newest planet-hunting mission.

name: TOI-700 e
significanceText: A second Earth-size habitable-zone world found in the very same system as TOI-700 d, discovered a year later once TESS gathered enough extra data — giving this one star two temperate, roughly Earth-sized planets to study side by side.
